result: TLR ligand-stimulated supernatants from THP-1 cells and PBMCs significantly reduced SARS-CoV-2 spike-induced cell-cell fusion, S2' cleavage, and syncytia formation in both spike-based fusion assays and authentic SARS-CoV-2 infection models. TLR ligands alone had no effect, demonstrating that soluble factors secreted by activated innate immune cells mediate this inhibition.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this finding, with one stating 'they demonstrate that soluble factors in the supernatants of TLR stimulated THP1 cells reduce fusion events' and another noting the authors 'used a cell-cell fusion assay developed previously to identify IL-1α/β as the cytokines that inhibit syncytia formation.' The bioluminescence assay is praised as 'a robust quantitative method.'

result: Through cytokine screening, IL-1α and IL-1β were identified as the key cytokines responsible for inhibiting SARS-CoV-2 spike-induced syncytia formation. Both cytokines significantly reduced bioluminescence signal, S2' cleavage, and syncytia area in spike-based fusion assays and authentic SARS-CoV-2 infection, with no synergistic effect when combined.
evaluation: Reviewers consistently affirm this identification, with one stating 'they convincingly demonstrate that recombinant IL-1 cytokines are sufficient to reduce cell-to-cell fusion mediated by the S protein' and another noting 'they used a cell-cell fusion assay developed previously to identify IL-1α/β as the cytokines that inhibit syncytia formation.' The study is described as identifying 'a new mechanism by which IL-1 cytokines can limit virus infection.'

result: IL-1RA treatment blocked the inhibitory effect of TLR-stimulated supernatants on cell-cell fusion. TLR2 was essential for IL-1β secretion in response to TLR2 ligands, and TLR2 knockout or TAK1/IKKβ inhibition in THP-1 cells prevented IL-1β secretion and eliminated the inhibitory effect on fusion.
evaluation: These findings are part of the mechanistic pathway that reviewers affirm. One reviewer notes the authors 'demonstrate that IL-1 cytokines are (not surprisingly) upregulated by TLR treatment in THP1 cells' using 'qRT-PCR and ELISA.' The pathway from TLR activation to IL-1β secretion is accepted as part of the overall mechanism.

result: IL-1β inhibited spike-induced cell-cell fusion across different SARS-CoV-2 variants (Alpha, Beta, Delta, Omicron) and other coronaviruses (SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV). Pre-treatment of either spike-expressing or ACE2-expressing cells with IL-1β reduced fusion, with additive effects when both cell types were pre-treated.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praise this breadth of testing. One states 'the authors tested IL-1 mediated inhibition of fusion induced by many different coronavirus S proteins and several SARS-CoV-2 strains' as a strength. Another notes 'diverse cell types and in vivo models were used, and consistent results were shown across diverse models.'

result: IL-1β inhibits SARS-CoV-2 spike-induced cell-cell fusion through the IL-1R1-MyD88-IRAK-TRAF6 pathway. Blocking any of these components (IL-1RA, MyD88 knockout, IRAK1/4 inhibitor, or TRAF6 knockout) eliminated IL-1β's inhibitory effect on fusion.
evaluation: Reviewers strongly affirm this mechanistic finding. One states 'they demonstrate that components of the myddosome (MYD88, IRAK1/4, and TRAF6) are required for fusion inhibition' and another notes 'they found that IL-1 prevents cell-cell fusion through MyD88/IRAK/TRAF6 but not TAK1/IKK/NF-κB.' This is described as revealing 'the inhibition of cell fusion did not require a transcriptional response and was mediated by IL-1R proximal signaling effectors.'

result: IL-1β inhibits SARS-CoV-2 spike-induced cell-cell fusion independent of the TAK1-IKKβ-NF-κB signaling cascade. IL-1β retained its inhibitory effect in TAK1 knockout cells, in the presence of IKKβ inhibitor, and after knockout of NF-κB pathway genes, demonstrating a non-canonical signaling mechanism.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. One states 'they demonstrate that components of the myddosome (MYD88, IRAK1/4, and TRAF6) are required for fusion inhibition, but that downstream canonical signaling (i.e., TAK1 and NFKB activation) is not required.' This is highlighted as revealing 'the inhibition of cell fusion did not require a transcriptional response.'

result: IL-1β activates RhoA signaling through a non-canonical IL-1 receptor-dependent pathway requiring MyD88 and TRAF6. IL-1β treatment caused RhoA activation and redistribution to cell-cell junctions, where it accumulated over time to prevent fusion, contrasting with the peripheral localization observed without IL-1β treatment.
evaluation: Reviewers strongly affirm this mechanism. One states 'the authors identified RhoA/ROCK activation by IL-1 as the basis for this inhibition of cell fusion. By visualizing a RhoA biosensor and actin, they found a redistribution of RhoA to the cell periphery and cell-cell junctions after IL-1 stimulation.' Another notes this is 'a non-canonical RhoA/ROCK signaling pathway' and describes it as 'convincing evidence.'

result: IL-1β drives the enrichment of actin bundles at cell-cell junctions through RhoA/ROCK activation, creating barriers that prevent membrane fusion. Constitutively active RhoA mimicked IL-1β's effect, while ROCK inhibitor Y-27632 prevented actin bundle formation and restored syncytia formation.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this mechanism. One states IL-1β 'triggered the formation of actin bundles at cell-cell junctions, preventing fusion and syncytia formation. The authors confirmed this molecular mechanism by using constitutively active RhoA and an inhibitor of ROCK.' Another notes 'the authors demonstrate that expression of a constitutively active RhoA alone is sufficient to inhibit fusion and that chemical inhibition of Rock could reverse this inhibition.'

result: During authentic SARS-CoV-2 infection, RhoA (visualized by GFP-AHPH) and F-actin relocalized away from cell-cell junctions and to the periphery during syncytia formation. IL-1β treatment reversed this, causing RhoA and actin bundles to accumulate at cell-cell junctions, preventing fusion. Constitutively active RhoA mimicked this effect in infected cells.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm these findings as part of the overall mechanism. One notes 'diverse cell types and in vivo models were used, and consistent results were shown across diverse models. These results were convincing and well-presented.' The consistency between spike-based and authentic infection models is implicitly accepted through the reviewers' overall positive assessment.

result: RhoA-CA and IL-1β treatment did not affect Spike protein binding to ACE2 or the distribution of ACE2 or Spike protein on the cell surface, indicating that the inhibition of fusion occurs through cytoskeletal rearrangement rather than receptor-ligand interaction.
evaluation: While not explicitly discussed by reviewers, this control experiment is implicitly accepted as part of the overall mechanism that reviewers describe as 'convincing' and 'well-presented.' The reviewers' acceptance of the RhoA/actin mechanism without questioning alternative explanations suggests these controls were adequate.

result: ROCK inhibitor Y-27632 promoted syncytia formation in a dose-dependent manner and abolished IL-1β's inhibitory effect on S2' cleavage, N protein levels, and actin bundle formation during authentic SARS-CoV-2 infection in multiple cell types including primary human lung cells.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm this finding as confirming the RhoA/ROCK mechanism. One states 'the authors demonstrate that expression of a constitutively active RhoA alone is sufficient to inhibit fusion and that chemical inhibition of Rock could reverse this inhibition.' The use of the ROCK inhibitor is accepted as validating the pathway.

result: In vivo infection experiments in mice confirmed that IL-1β treatment significantly reduced body weight loss, pulmonary injury, viral N gene expression, and infected area in lung tissue during SARS-CoV-2 infection. IL-1β induced actin bundle formation at cell-cell junctions in infected lung epithelial cells, restricting syncytia formation and viral transmission. IL-1RA co-treatment abolished these protective effects.
evaluation: Reviewers strongly affirm these in vivo findings. One states 'in vivo infection experiments in mice confirmed that IL-1β significantly restricted SARS-CoV-2 spread in the lung epithelium' and notes 'the authors demonstrate that recombinant IL-1 can reduce viral burden and lung pathogenesis in a mouse model of infection.' Another states this 'suggests that this process may also function to inhibit SARS-CoV-2 infection in vivo.'

result: IL-1β treatment did not cause toxicity in uninfected mice (no changes in body weight, liver, or spleen weight) and conferred lasting protective effects, as tissue cells isolated from IL-1β-treated mice remained resistant to SARS-CoV-2 infection ex vivo.
evaluation: While not explicitly discussed, these safety and durability findings are implicitly accepted as part of the in vivo validation that reviewers describe positively. The reviewers' overall assessment of the in vivo work as 'convincing' suggests these supporting data were adequate.

result: Y-27632 treatment abolished IL-1β's protective effects in vivo, compromising prevention of weight loss, aggravating lung injury, increasing viral N gene expression and infected area, and preventing actin bundle formation. This confirmed that IL-1β prevents SARS-CoV-2 transmission through the RhoA/ROCK pathway in vivo.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this in vivo validation of the mechanism. One states 'use of a ROCK inhibitor in IL-1 treated mice restored the ability of SARS-CoV-2 to spread in the lung, suggesting that this inhibitory process functions in vivo' and another notes 'the authors demonstrate that recombinant IL-1 mediated inhibition of SARS-CoV-2 infection in mice is dependent on the RhoA/Rock pathway.'
